chapters.summary: Cabán describes a secondary mental health crisis driven by fear and care disruption. Taylor Brown says untreated gender dysphoria worsens over time and cites a Nature study finding a 72% increase in suicide attempts in states with anti-trans laws.
chapters.title: Cabán asks about mental health harms when care is delayed or denied

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I mean, again, I know that

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: at large, the TGNBI community is on high alert and

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: understandably cautious about what they're divulging even to these resources in this moment in time, and that's because of the current political environment and the attacks from the federal level.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: To that end, the political environment has created what many clinicians describe as a secondary mental health crisis.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Separate from any underlying gender dysphoria that's driven by fear, uncertainty, the experience of having care disrupted or threatened.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And we hit the pieces around, you know, it's not a person's gender identity that is...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: The cause of mental health stress or distress, but the treatment from others that they receive around that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then now we're layering on top these other fears because of the political environment.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can you talk about the evidence show, what evidence?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: shows about mental health outcomes when care is delayed, when it's interrupted, when it's denied, compared to when it is accessible.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And is DOHMH communicating that to providers and families?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And very quickly before you answer, just want to acknowledge that we have been joined by Councilmember Brooks-Powers.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, thanks.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to hand it over to Director Brown to kick us off.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Thank you for the question, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: We know that undiagnosed, untreated, and undertreated gender dysphoria often becomes more severe over time, leading to further exacerbation of both physical and mental health disparities and risk with age.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: This is similar to any chronic health condition that is left untreated or when care is interrupted.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: A recent study published in Nature highlights the devastating impacts of anti-trans legislation in states,

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: finding that these bans, a collection of laws that restrict rights, including access to gender-affirming health care, have led to a 72% increase in suicide attempts among transgender and non-binary people compared to states without such legislation.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: These findings are also supported by an article analyzing several more recent studies published by the American Psychological Association as well.

chapters.summary: Cabán shares her own experience with a chronic condition and asks about protective factors beyond medical care. Davidoff names family support and affirmation, caring adults, peers, teachers, youth development, and community safety as protective against depression, suicidality, and substance use.
chapters.title: Cabán asks DOHMH about protective factors for TGNB youth mental health

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I really appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And just to underscore that this is something that's not unique across the board in that sense.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: There are tons of people who are being denied access to mental health care for a number of reasons, again, at the hands of the federal government and the distress that

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: that causes, I am somebody who lives with a chronic health condition and the period of time it took to get a diagnosis and the difficulty of being seen and heard and really taken seriously and treated was,

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: it was a really, really difficult time as

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: an adult with access to consistent mental health care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And still, I struggled immensely.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And so I cannot imagine what young folks are struggling with when they're not sure where they can get their care.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions and I'm going to hand it over to my co-chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But beyond medical care, what does DOHMH understand to be the most important protective factors for TGNB youth mental health?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Just as examples, such as family acceptance, affirming schools, community connection, things like that.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: There are many protective factors, and I'd say the most widely protective factor is connectedness to parents.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: So family support and affirmation is absolutely critical as a protective factor.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Others include connectedness to other, you know, adults, caring adults, adult relatives, adults in the community,

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: peers and friends, teachers, youth development opportunities, and feeling safe in the community.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Those were all protective factors.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: And I'm looking at, and that goes for, you know, transgender, genderqueer, genderfluid, questioning youth.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: And these were protective factors against depression, suicidality, and substance use.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks Davidoff to flesh out the idea of connectedness. Davidoff says it means being seen and affirmed in gender identity and pronouns, and that affirmation and support are central to connectedness.
chapters.title: Cabán and Davidoff discuss what connectedness means for trans youth

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can you go into, can you flesh out those, that sort of definition of connectedness for folks?

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, I think that the definition of connectedness is tied into the idea of affirmation and support.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: So it's being seen for who you are, the gender identity that you are choosing to present as, the pronouns you're choosing to use, that those are all affirmed and supported.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: And that's a critical part, I think, of that connectedness factor.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, obviously there's a large scope of what parental responsibility looks like and how.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: children, even when we're adults, because we still carry that.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: parent relationship trauma around like, you know, differences between being fed and housed and being emotionally supported and seen and understood, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So thank you for fleshing that out.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I appreciate it.

chapters.summary: Cabán cites research that family acceptance reduces suicide risk and asks about programming for parents. Davidoff describes Family Youth Peer Support Alliances in each borough and the Strong Families and Communities Training Center, with Queens and Staten Island alliances doing focused work.
chapters.title: Cabán asks about DOHMH resources for parents and caregivers of TGNB youth

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And then my last question before handing it over to Chair Narcissus, you mentioned that parental support is one of the strongest protective factors for mental health, the mental health of transgender youth and

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: research consistently shows that family acceptance dramatically reduces suicide risk.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So does DOHMH have any programming or resources specifically designed to support parents and caregivers of TGNB youth, both in understanding the mental health benefits of affirming care and in navigating the current climate of misinformation?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if not, is there a capacity to develop that?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And again, before you answer, I want to acknowledge that we have been joined by Councilmember Lee.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Yes, so the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene supports a set of programs that offer both family peer support and youth peer support.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: We have, we call them the Family Youth Peer Support Alliances.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: There is one per borough.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: There's also a training and technical assistance center associated with these alliances.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: And the training center, the Strong Families and Communities Training Center, has been providing trainings to all of our peer advocates on working with LGBTQ youth and their families and to help them to navigate related systems

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: and to provide the variety of peer supports that are needed.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Specifically, we've had a lot of focus among the Queens Alliance provider and the Staten Island Alliance provider have really been doing a lot of work in this area,

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: including running groups for individuals and their families and really building their capacity to serve.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Shout out to Staten Island.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I have a few more questions, but I'm going to pass it over to Chair Narcisse.

chapters.summary: Narcisse frames the hearing around fairness, support, and access to care. She asks what H&H clinical experience shows; Omar Fattal says research and evidence show affirming care lowers depression and suicidality and improves overall mental well-being.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks H&H about mental health outcomes with stable affirming care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Two things as I'm sitting here and processing about life is acceptable in society that we live in and accessible to the best health care that you can get.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: as a human being.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: It's treating each other fairly, and unfortunately that we have, like my colleague just mentioned, you have difficulty and you don't have that support.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we want to see New York City is a place where we support one another, and it's very important for us to be mindful of what's going on in our society.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So I thank you for being here and answering our question.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Mental health, unless we talk about the service capacity and mental health continuity.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Mental health, what does H&H clinical experience show about mental health outcomes for youth once they have stable access to gender-affirming care?

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Hi, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: I can't comment on individual cases, but I can agree with everything that was said before me.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: There's research and evidence that shows that access to gender-affirming care does improve overall mental health outcomes, including lowering depression, lowering suicidality, and improving overall mental well-being.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about clinician capacity for TGNB patients. Fattal says H&H child and adolescent behavioral services have capacity across boroughs, patients can be referred internally or call 1-844-NYC4NYC, and Narcisse praises H&H for not turning people away.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks whether H&H has enough licensed mental health clinicians

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Does H&H have enough licensed mental health clinicians to serve TGNB patients?

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yes, I'm happy to share that we do have capacity to, in our child and adolescent behavioral services, we offer the whole spectrum of services for children and adolescents in all boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: And we welcome all New Yorkers, including LGBTQ plus patients.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: And we've made it very easy for people to access care in our system.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Two ways.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: One is that they can be referred by their medical team, and their medical team can connect them internally to behavioral services, or people can call on their own.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: It's one number, the contact center.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: I can mention it, 1-844-NYC4NYC, and all they have to say is, I want to be connected to behavioral services, and we take care of it from there.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And by the way, I'm very proud of H&H providing those services because we know when other hospital facilities are not receiving patients, H&H, you know, if you're listening to know that H&H is on your side, the city hospital never turned people away.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks about the value of coordinating mental health support with affirming care. Wallach cites his 29 years at H&H and integrated physical and behavioral health programs; Fattal says H&H connects patients internally between primary care and behavioral health.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks H&H about coordinating mental health with gender-affirming care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: What does HNH see as the value of coordinating mental health support with gender-affirming care?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Yeah, great.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Thank you for those comments and for the particular question.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: I have to say I'm entering my 29th year working at New York City Health and Hospitals as an internist.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And one of the things I most...

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: proud about our healthcare system is its longstanding history of integration of both physical and behavioral health services through programs like collaborative care and primary care, which focuses on depression and anxiety.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And I would say that coordinating gender-affirming care with mental health support as clinically necessary and, of course, with informed consent, we know and we've heard leads to better mental health outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So here at New York City Health and Hospitals, this is absolutely a process that we use to provide full care to the patient.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: But I'm going to turn it over back to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Fattal for additional comment.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yeah, I agree 100%.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: And we do it on behalf of the patient, so we don't rely on the patient to have to connect the dots.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: So if the patient is already engaged in treatment in primary care, primary care team would make the referral to behavioral health, and the reverse is true.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: If someone starts their care in behavioral health and we realize that they need medical services, then we connect them with medical services internally.

chapters.summary: Narcisse says she works for H&H as a nurse and believes in the care provided, and mentions Elmhurst never turning anyone away. Fattal jokes that H&H does not mind her being biased.
chapters.title: Narcisse discloses H&H employment and praises public hospital care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And for disclosure, I work for H&H as a nurse, so I don't want people to think I'm biased.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Let's be clear, I work and then I believe in the care that you're providing.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And if I may say, it was Elmer's Hospital, which would never turn anyone away.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We don't mind you being biased.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks whether staff have observed increased anxiety among patients and families. Wallach says H&H is hearing rumblings from patients and aims to reassure through updated public websites, social media, patient emails, and exam-room communication.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks if staff see increased anxiety over federal and Medicaid changes

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Have staff observed increased anxiety among patients and families about the federal environment or Medicaid changes?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Yeah, you know, it's hard again, as Dr.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Fattal said, I'm going to go to comment.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: On specific patients, but I would say broadly speaking.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Broadly.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: We are starting to hear rumblings from the patients to whom we provide care.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: However, from our perspective, it is always, always our hope that H&H creates an environment of support and reassurance for all patients, including those seeking gender-affirming care.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And as such, shout out to my colleagues at H&H who really do a fantastic job of updating guidance on our public-facing websites and our social media channels,

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: as well as through patient emails and during visits of patients in the exam room with the care teams to make sure that they feel safe and they're provided with all the necessary information because we know getting accurate

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: and correct information is critical.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: That's right.

chapters.summary: Narcisse asks how H&H involves and supports parents and caregivers, given family acceptance's protective role. Fattal says child and adolescent behavioral services include families and caregivers, H&H works in 50 schools, and the same approach applies to LGBTQ patients.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks how H&H supports parents and caregivers as protective factors

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And we have been joined by my colleagues, Wilson, in the house.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: How does H&H involve and support parents and caregivers, giving the role of family acceptance as a protective factor?

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yeah, for all our child and adolescent behavioral services, including the family, the legal guardian, the other caregivers involved in the care of the patient, is core to what we do in treating all our patients.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: And this is definitely true in the case of LGBTQ patients and in the case of providing gender-affirming care.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: While we're at it, do we create a support system for the family specifically?

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Because we know.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: in some culture is more difficult for acceptance.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And that's the reason when I started, I talk about acceptance and accessible and where we are in life.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yeah, definitely.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We have this in mental health in general because there's a lot of stigma and there's a lot of resistance sometimes from families, communities.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: So we're used to doing that.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We're very used to including other caregivers, including the communities.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We do a lot of work, for example, in schools.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We're present in 50 schools in New York where we provide mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: So we have this as part of the way we provide services for children and adolescents, and we apply the same when dealing with gender-affirming care or when working with LGBTQ patients.

chapters.summary: Narcisse describes ER experience where family beliefs can obstruct care for young people. Fattal says H&H treats the whole person including family, while practicing within New York State OMH guidelines and regulations.
chapters.title: Narcisse follows up on families who obstruct gender-affirming care

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So if a family actually come with the young folks and they are not as kind of like not in a place where they, because what I have found in my time

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: in the ER, sometimes they can be an obstruction for you because of their belief or whatever it may be.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: So do you kind of like providing that kind of support right away to make sure the family kind of have an understanding and more kind of like helping with the process of providing the care for that young person?

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yeah, 100%.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We treat the whole person.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We don't look only at the mental health side of things.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We look at the...

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: whole person and treating the whole person includes including their family and involving them.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: I do have to say that we practice within all four corners of the law and we practice within the New York State OMH guidelines and regulations.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: So obviously we do all of this within the available guidelines that we have.

chapters.summary: Narcisse notes Pride centers are mostly in Manhattan, the Bronx, and Brooklyn and asks about expansion as private hospitals pull back. Wallach cites telehealth, system-wide referrals, and lists Pride sites including Lincoln, Bellevue, Woodhull, Metropolitan, Elmhurst, Jacoby, Gotham Gouverneur, and Gotham Judson.
chapters.title: Narcisse asks about expanding Pride Health access in Staten Island and Queens

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Pride Health Centers.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: The four Pride Health Centers are primarily located in Manhattan, the Bronx, and Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: For TGNB, New Yorkers in Staten Island or out of Queens,

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: distance can be a meaningful barrier, particularly now that same private hospitals programs have pulled back.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Are there any plans to expand access points even for mental health services specifically in those boroughs?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So I can start and then I'll pass it back to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Fattal.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And thank you for that question.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: I would say the last time I was sitting in this room was during the COVID pandemic, giving testimony.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And if we were to look back historically, I'm a kind of a glass half full kind of guy, that one of the positives that came out of the pandemic

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: was our ability to turn on telehealth or virtual care literally overnight in the midst of the pandemic.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And one of the things, again, that I'm very proud of New York City Health and Hospitals is our continuation of those services to, as I said before, reach New Yorkers where they want to be met.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: We have relied very much on telehealth or virtual care to reach patients throughout all five boroughs in the city.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Now, to your question, I would say we continuously monitor.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: The need or the demand for clinical services throughout our system and indeed we work as a system right so i want to be very clear that a system works in that not all services are available

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: at each and every center but as a system we work together so if i'm seeing patients at bellevue and i don't have a particular service there i can refer that patient

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: to one of our other facilities.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And telehealth is absolutely a tool for convenience.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And I would say, and I was going to turn it over to you, Amar, but certainly in the behavioral health realm lends itself very nicely to that exact type of care.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So maybe if you have additional comment.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yeah, 100%.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: This is one of the few things that the good things that came out of COVID is really transformed the way we deliver care.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We've actually published studies on this from H&H where we saw higher show rates for people who are using telehealth.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: So we very much use that.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: And as Dr.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Wallach mentioned, in behavioral health, if you think about it, most of what we do is based on talk therapy, and we don't really need to touch a person or do a physical exam.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: So it lends itself very nicely to telehealth.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And Chairman and Nurses, if I may, just to say we offer a Pride Center at Lincoln, Bellevue, Woodhull, Metropolitan, Elmhurst, and Jacoby.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: In addition, there are two additional sites as well.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So it's not just four sites within our system.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Gotham Health, both Gouverneur and Gotham Health Judson.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Narcisse thanks H&H for its support and advocates for keeping New York City health care available to all. She passes the mic back to Chair Cabán.
chapters.title: Narcisse thanks H&H and advocates, passes to Chair Cabán

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I want to say thank you for all your support and the advocates in the room to continue making sure that New York City, when it comes to health care, is for all of us.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: No matter where you're from, no matter what gender, just hold New York City together.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: Thank you for your service.

utterances.speaker: Mercedes Narcisse
utterances.text: And I'll pass it back to Mike Ali.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I'll go ahead and pass it over to Chair Farias.

chapters.summary: Farías asks whether the NYC Youth Risk Behavior Survey or other DOHMH surveys capture gender identity. Davidoff confirms the YRBS for high school and middle school public school students captures gender identity data.
chapters.title: Farías asks whether NYC surveys capture gender identity

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and thanks for all of your testimony this morning, folks.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Just really quickly on local data, does NYC Youth Risk Behavior Survey or any other DOHMH survey capture gender identity specifically?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Someone on the panel, you want to come back up?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Yes, the Youth Risk Behavior Survey for both high school and middle school New York City public school students does capture data on gender identity.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what the gender identity data show on depression, anxiety, self-harm, and suicide. Davidoff says disparities exist and cites 2023 suicidal ideation rates: trans 42%, nonbinary 38%, other gender identity 45%, questioning 28%, and cisgender 16%.
chapters.title: Farías asks what YRBS shows on TGNB youth mental health disparities

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, and since we do capture that data, what does it show, if at all, anything around depression, anxiety, self-harm, suicide attempts or ideations among TGNB youth compared to their cisgender counterparts?

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Yeah, it shows health disparities for sure.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: So it shows that students who identify as transgender are more likely to report electronic bullying, feeling persistent sadness or hopelessness, suicide ideation, and suicide attempts than cisgender students.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: So for example, in the

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: 2023, we saw that public high school students who identified as transgender or non-binary or some other gender identity or questioning were more likely to report suicide ideation.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: So those groups were 40, the groups, sorry, let me say this differently.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: The percentage of each of those populations that reported suicide ideation were for transgender was 42%.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: For non-binary, it was 38%.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: Those who said that they identified as some other gender, it was 45%.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: And those who identified as questioning, it was 28%.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: That's, again, the percentage who reported suicidal ideation versus those who identified as cisgender.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: It was 16%.

utterances.speaker: Marnie Davidoff
utterances.text: So that's just we have data on the various outcomes, but that's just one example that illustrates the disparity.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what immediate support exists for a young person or family after care disruption, before a formal complaint. Brown discusses state inpatient discharge rights and professional continuity-of-care rules, but says there is no clear city analog and may follow up.
chapters.title: Farías asks about support after care disruption under LGBTQ Healthcare Bill of Rights

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'd like to talk a little bit about the NYC LGBTQ Healthcare Bill of Rights.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: We know the Bill of Rights directs individuals who experience discrimination or denial of care to file complaints through the NYC Human Rights Commission.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Can you walk us through what support, if any, is available to a young person or their family in the immediate aftermath of a care disruption or before a formal complaint process actually gets underway?

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Yes, I'll briefly touch on this.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I just want to clarify, Chair Farias, you're speaking about a patient who is discharged and immediately prior to filing a complaint,

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: you know, in the event that they need medication or ongoing services.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yes, and what the process is prior to in terms of referring directly to the Bill of Rights that we have in the city.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Yeah, and so, you know, my understanding of this, and I think we, you know, we may have to get back to you, but I'll pass it back to my colleagues, too, if they have additional information.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so the way that I thought about this question, I'll say is that my understanding, I guess, of

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: New York state law, anyway, in regards to patients who are in an inpatient hospital setting, they actually do have certain enumerated rights in regards to discharge and continuation of care and continuity of care.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: I'm unaware at this time of a similar sort of analog in relation to city law, and that may just be because of regulatory purview.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: But I will say sort of in a private clinic, all physicians are licensed and regulated by the state board, and professional rules for physicians

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: expressly state that it is professional misconduct.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: malpractice to discharge a patient without figuring out a plan to make in a reasonable amount of time to make sure

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: that they are going to be able to find a provider and ensure continuity of care and they also need to be available in that time to provide care and on an emergency basis.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I'm not sure if my colleagues have any other, anything else to add on that point.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Oh, wonderful, sorry.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I would also assume not only in timeframe, but also potentially in the language they speak, et cetera, they're receiving whatever after, like whatever care needs to come, right?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Like we're also, I just wanna throw it out there that we should also be making sure we're

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Bilingual, which I'm making the assumption that we are in terms of aftermath care.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: I mean, I believe our language access rules would require that.

chapters.summary: Staff swears in another witness who cites the $15 million investment's call and text line as a backstop linking New Yorkers to care. Farías asks for concrete steps and bilingual aftercare; Brown says city language access rules would require that.
chapters.title: Farías questions city call/text line and language access after care disruption

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: We're just going to swear you in before you contribute.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, you may answer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: In addition to what...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: The director shared is that, you know, we're also really excited to be utilizing a portion of the $15 million investment to launch the call and text line to act as an appropriate and as an important backstop for New Yorkers

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public
utterances.text: to link them to care services and information and resources related to gender affirming care.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay, so I guess I'll follow up after the hearing.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I just kind of want to better understand what are the actual steps.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I mean, we do a lot of this throughout the city of New York, depending on what agency it is, and I'd like to know what the steps that we have in place to ensure that that care is underway and actually being performed.

chapters.summary: Farías asks Brown to connect her litigation background to the office's current work. Brown describes prior roles at the NYS Attorney General's Civil Rights Bureau, ACLU, and Lambda Legal, doing impact litigation for transgender people, and says that experience informs using legal tools amid federal hostility.
chapters.title: Farías asks Director Brown how litigation experience shapes LGBTQ+ initiatives

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Let's see.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I'd like to talk about, I mean specifically Director Brown, if you can speak a little bit about your litigation experience and how that's informing the initiatives the office is undertaking in the current

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: federal environment that we have here.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I feel like you spoke a little bit to that in your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Would just like to hear how you're framing or the framework of the initiatives coming out of the office.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you for the question.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so for those who don't know, prior to this position, I was an assistant attorney general in the Civil Rights Bureau here in the office of the New York State Attorney General, Letitia James.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Before that, I was a staff attorney at both the American Civil Liberties Union and Lambda Legal.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I was doing impact litigation on behalf of transgender people across the country.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I graduated from law school in 2017, so that was right when Trump was elected, so I really cut my teeth in doing a lot of that very early litigation as well as it continued on.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so I would say,

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And my work specifically was focused on health care in a very real way because of my own sort of personal story in that.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so because of the types of cases I led and their significance, that has given me deep expertise in both civil rights and constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: I think it also has given me, clearly, but even from a personal perspective, but a very deep understanding of the issues facing LGBTQIA people and especially where those issues intersect with government.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: My office's work is done in the shadow of unprecedented federal hostility and serious changes to the legal landscape.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so in the shadow of that, my litigation experience, primarily suing governmental entities and actors and challenging unconstitutional or unlawful executive orders, laws,

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: policies, regulations, and what have you, it's given me a deep understanding because we also have those tools.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so it has given me a deep understanding of how to use those tools and others that government has in order to effectuate true change in people's lives for the better.

chapters.summary: Farías asks what legal developments Brown is watching and how the Council can help. Brown says she monitors the federal register, Supreme Court docket, and litigation, flags data as a key area likely needing legislative solutions, and wants to meet LGBTQI people in Council districts.
chapters.title: Farías asks what federal actions the office tracks and what Council support is needed

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Are there any federal actions or legal developments that you're planning or the office is planning to watch more closely or track?

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: You know, I think that is something, I consider that an obligation of my office.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: I think I'm often in contact with my colleagues and work closely with my colleagues in the Office of Chief Counsel as well as the law department in monitoring any

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: legal, regulatory, and especially federal action, I guess, tweet at this point, that could potentially impact LGBTQIA people.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: So that is something, and again, so that goes to things like federal register, tracking the Supreme Court docket, and also just looking at litigations in both our federal and state courts.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And is there anything that comes to mind in terms of council support, whether that's for the office, for any of the initiatives, or any of the...

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Federal level legal items that you folks are going to be tracking and watching, any support that can be coming from the council side?

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Yeah, and again, so at a certain point I won't be able to reference my relatively short tenure,

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: but I will say at this stage preliminarily, not so much on that, and thinking about some of the sort of planning that I'm doing, one thing that's coming up for me and has been coming up for me in my practice as a civil rights litigator

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: is the issue of data, and I think we've been referencing that today.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I do believe that that could and probably likely would require a legislative fix, or not fix, but solutions and innovation, I guess I should say.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: At a very high level, when we work towards solutions for systemic issues affecting historically and intentionally marginalized communities, data is key for many reasons, including evincing the problem, understanding the scale of interventions required,

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: formulating solutions, monitoring their efficacy.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: I should also say, and I'm also very eager to hear from you all and to meet with LGBTQI people in your districts to understand their needs and what's impacting them as well.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so I just want to say that to you all.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for the responses today.

chapters.summary: Cabán thanks Farías for asking about collaboration opportunities. She says the Council has passed TGNC and NBI protections and funding, and is ready to partner with the administration on innovation.
chapters.title: Cabán offers Council as eager partner for LGBTQ+ policy innovation

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'll kick it back over to Chair Kavanaugh.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, and I deeply appreciate Chair Fetty has questions around collaboration opportunities with council.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Just to, if it wasn't already clear, you have really, really eager, willing partners in the council.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We passed a number of TGNC-NBI protections at the municipal level.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We've worked together, obviously, in getting funding for our community, and so we're here to be partners in that innovation.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks how the Mayor's Office of LGBTQ Affairs coordinates with other agencies and whether it will outreach hospitals about youth affirming care. Brown describes cooperation with CCHR, the Law Department, OCH, DOHMH, and H&H, plus planning around H.R. 1 and public awareness.
chapters.title: Cabán asks about Mayor's Office coordination and outreach to hospitals

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to follow up on this line of questioning that the chair just engaged in.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: What is the mayor's office of LGBTQ affairs, the coordination with other agencies look like?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: You started to touch on it, but if you could go into some more specifics around it and will you be doing...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Any outreach to hospitals about the benefits of providing access to gender-affirming care to youth and mental health impacts?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Is it a situation where, like, they already know, and so maybe that's not necessary?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But, yeah, I'd be curious to know.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, that cooperation began.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: on day one of my tenure in this position.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I think that, and I know that that comes from a fundamental belief that government services are for all people in New York, including LGBTQIA people.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so, you know, my office, I think of it as a way to ensure that agencies are providing those services that are inclusive of LGBTQIA people who are sometimes often, you know, not thought of or, you know, solutions aren't sort of centered.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so just off the top of my head, I can say I've had many conversations with CCHR, law department, OCH, my wonderful colleagues at both health and hospitals and the Department of Health.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And I'm planning other things to work with fellow agency and office heads.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And so, yeah, I mean, I think that just has to be built into my work because, again, those especially, you know, when we're talking about agencies dedicated to homeless prevention, health care, housing, what have you, those are all LGBTQIA issues.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And thus, my community must be taken into account in those decisions.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And also sharing the important work that those offices are doing.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: I think sometimes the public may not have an awareness that those offices may be for them and are required to serve them as well.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And it brings to mind, too, I just had a conversation with Commissioner Martin from the Department of Health who is planning some things around H.R.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And that's something that is certain.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: going to impact LGBTQIA people.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: So we've had conversations about sort of how do we get more information to the communities that I serve specifically.

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: And apologies, could you please repeat the second part of your question?

utterances.speaker: Taylor Brown
utterances.text: Or was there a second part?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I think you very, very thoroughly answered the question.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I'm going to hand it over to colleagues, but I just, as you say that, you know, the council's LGBTQIA plus caucus obviously has, for the past several years, been putting out a policy plan and roadmap.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And I want to give a really, really big shout out and acknowledgement to now Councilmember Wilson, who at the time was the Chief of Staff to Councilmember Botcher, and really, really anchored a lot of the work that we did on the Pride and Policy

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: report.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: There is an updated version of that coming out soon, but I think that's also an area for us to be able to collaborate, and we can be talking about legislative interventions.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But is Wilson next?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Oh, because he's not here.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Carl Wilson asks how the city assesses capacity and mental health impacts when major hospital systems stop youth affirming care. Wallach says H&H monitors demand and capacity and stands ready to support all patients; Fattal says mental health capacity exists and gives the contact center number.
chapters.title: Council Member Wilson asks H&H how hospital exits affect capacity and tracking

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And with that, I'll pass it over to Councilmember Wilson.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Appreciate those comments.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Hi there.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I have a, for H&H, when a major hospital system stops providing gender-affirming care for youth, how does the city assess the resulting impact on both

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: hospital capacity and the mental health of the affected patients and who is responsible for tracking those outcomes.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Yeah, so I'll start and then I'll pass it over to Dr.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Vital.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And just to say, it's hard for us to comment on what the private hospitals are doing, but we stand, as we've said in our testimony, at the ready to fully support all patients in need of care, no exceptions.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And so as part of any other type of care that New York City Health and Hospitals provides, whether it's cardiology or GYN services, we regularly monitor what that demand is, and we look at our capacity within our system, and we adjust

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: what is available to patients.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So it's no different for gender-affirming care, and it's something that we keep a close look at.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Yeah, exactly.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Same thing for mental health.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: Our mission is to serve all New Yorkers without exception.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: And I'm happy to say that we do have capacity in mental health right now.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: We've made it very easy for New Yorkers who are looking for help to get it.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: This is for all New Yorkers, including LGBTQ plus people.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: One number, 1-844-NYC for NYC.

utterances.speaker: Omar Fattal
utterances.text: All they have to do is ask to be connected to behavioral services, and we can connect them to care.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks about system-wide safeguards during policy uncertainty. Wallach says H&H has not changed its scope of practice for gender-affirming care.
chapters.title: Wilson asks about safeguards against abrupt interruptions in medically necessary care

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Are there system-wide safeguards that help ensure patients do not experience abrupt interruptions in medically necessary care, especially during periods of policy uncertainty?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So I can start again on that.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And I would say they have been known.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And if there's anything that you need to get back to us on, let's find two.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: But just to say, we have not changed our scope of practice for gender-affirming care at New York City Health and Hospitals.

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Wilson asks whether H&H will notify the Council of significant policy changes affecting equitable access without unnecessary clinical detail. Wallach emphasizes HIPAA, patient rights, annual compliance training, and following law on release of information.
chapters.title: Wilson asks H&H to notify Council of policy changes while protecting privacy

utterances.speaker: Carl Wilson
utterances.text: I guess I would just say, can H&H commit to notifying the council of any significant policy changes affecting equitable access in a manner that protects patient privacy and avoids unnecessary clinical or operational detail?

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: Yeah, so again, privacy and patient rights is critical to health care.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: It is a partnership between the patient and the care team.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: And so we certainly adhere to all regulations and rules, specifically HIPAA, and do everything we can within the bounds of the law as far as release of information.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So it is something that we take very seriously.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: As a member of the health and hospitals community, we have annual compliance update that all staff members must go through in addition to the trainings.

utterances.speaker: Andrew Wallach
utterances.text: So this is something that is very near and dear and important to us.

chapters.summary: Cabán notes the Health Map's LGBTQ health services portal and asks how often provider information is verified. Andrea Howard is sworn in and says the section launched in 2018, participation is voluntary, and DOHMH is reviewing and surveying providers, including updating Mount Sinai and NYU listings.
chapters.title: Cabán questions DOHMH on NYC Health Map maintenance and provider verification

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I have, I think, just two more questions at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: I want to touch on the New York City Health Map.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: We have it, right?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So it currently features a dedicated LGBTQ health services portal that allows New Yorkers to search for providers by geographic proximity and medical need.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Can you talk a little bit about how the map is maintained and specifically how frequently provider information is verified and updated?

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Please raise your right hand.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Do you affirm to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth before these committees and to respond honestly to council member questions?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Sorry, yes I do.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: My name is Andrea Howard.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: I'm the Deputy Commissioner for Disease Control at the New York City Health Department, and I use the pronouns she, her.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: So the LGBTQ health services are a section of the health map, and that was first launched, this particular section, in 2018.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And since that time, it's gone ad hoc updates.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Participation is voluntary, and providers have to consent to their information being included in the health map.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: And participating providers are responsible for informing the health department when that information needs to be updated because of contact information changes or services change.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Now, recognizing that that is not always done,

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Particularly in light of the recent changing care landscape, we're undertaking a comprehensive review of this section.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: This will include surveying all providers that are currently included in the health map to make sure that they continue to provide culturally competent and affirmative services and that the information is accurate.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: We'll also be reaching out to additional providers.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Through consultation with our networks to see if they would like to be included.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Now, in the interim, we have reached out to certain providers when we know that services have been changed.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: For example, we reached out to Mount Sinai and to NYU facilities, and we revised their listing to reflect that they no longer offer gender-affirming care to youth.

chapters.summary: Cabán says DOHMH is relying on providers to report changes and asks about other ways to verify accuracy. Howard says a comprehensive survey is planned for the fall and asks the Council to flag inaccuracies; Cabán suggests proactive outreach to advocacy groups.
chapters.title: Cabán presses DOHMH on directory accuracy and resources

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Yeah, I think you're acknowledging sort of the gap that people can proactively tell you things are changing, but some people you're going to end up having to chase down.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Obviously, NYU, Mount Sinai, that's...

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: It was big news, so it was easy to track that down.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: But are there other ways that you're looking into whether the directory is accurate?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And how often are you finding that you're doing it or that you think it necessitates doing?

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And also, how is that process being resourced?

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: Yeah, so as I mentioned, we're currently planning to launch a survey later this fall so we can do a content.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: comprehensive update.

utterances.speaker: Andrea Howard
utterances.text: In the meantime, if any of you know of any information that is inaccurate, please let us know and we can reach out to the provider and verify.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: Okay, great.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: And, you know, I think even in terms of being proactive, obviously there are lots of organizations, service providers, advocacy groups that are on the ground and

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: have relationships with families that are navigating this in real time.

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
utterances.text: So I think that also might be a good place to do some proactive outreach to get that information more quickly.

chapters.summary: Cabán asks if the map indicates which providers offer gender-affirming care for youth separately from adults. Howard says users can filter by primary care, gender-affirming care, sexual health, and behavioral health, and by adult or youth services.
chapters.title: Cabán asks whether Health Map distinguishes youth from adult affirming care

utterances.speaker: Tiffany L. Cabán
